clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia defined by the triad of nail dystrophy, palmoplantar keratoderma and hair defects
Caused by variants in GJB6, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin 30
Crucially, sweating is normal (hidrotic), distinguishing it from the anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasias where heat intolerance is a major concern
Nail changes are prominent, with thickened, slow-growing, discoloured and dystrophic nails that are prone to infection
Hair is sparse, fine and brittle, with partial or total alopecia of the scalp, eyebrows and body hair
A diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and hyperpigmentation over the knuckles and other bony prominences are common
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by family history and GJB6 molecular testing; management is supportive with nail, hair and keratoderma care
reference.pathophysiology: Clouston syndrome is caused by dominant variants in GJB6, encoding connexin 30, a gap-junction protein that forms intercellular channels in the epidermis and its appendages. Defective connexin 30 impairs communication between keratinocytes and disturbs the development and maintenance of ectodermal structures derived from surface ectoderm, namely nails, hair and the palmoplantar epidermis. Because eccrine sweat glands are relatively spared, sweating remains normal, which clinically separates this hidrotic dysplasia from the anhidrotic forms caused by defects in the ectodysplasin pathway.
additionalInvestigations: Nail assessment and mycological sampling for secondary onychomycosis
Assessment of palmoplantar keratoderma and function
Dental and audiological review to help distinguish from other ectodermal dysplasias
redFlags: Painful fissuring of palmoplantar keratoderma impairing function
Features atypical for a hidrotic dysplasia suggesting an alternative syndrome
Significant psychosocial impact from alopecia and nail changes
reference.prognosis: The condition is compatible with a normal lifespan and, because sweating is preserved, lacks the heat-intolerance risks of anhidrotic dysplasias; the main burden is cosmetic and from nail and keratoderma complications.
pitfalls: Confusing it with anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia and warning unnecessarily about heat intolerance
Overlooking secondary onychomycosis superimposed on dystrophic nails
Attributing hair loss to a primary alopecia rather than the ectodermal dysplasia
Neglecting genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition
management: Topical management of the palmoplantar keratoderma with emollients and keratolytics such as urea or salicylic acid, with topical or oral retinoids for severe hyperkeratosis.
Nail care with regular chiropody and treatment of secondary fungal infection with antifungal agents.
Cosmetic support for alopecia, including wigs or hairpieces, alongside gentle scalp care.
Periodic dermatological review of skin, hair and nails to detect and treat complications.
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant connexin-30 (GJB6) disorder, with assessment of at-risk relatives.
Reassurance that sweating is preserved, so the heat-intolerance precautions of anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia are unnecessary, with psychological support for the cosmetic burden.
